{{Short description|Classified joint CIA–NSA program to insert eavesdropping equipment in difficult places}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=September 2024}}
[[File:Special Collection Service 11.jpg|thumb|Locations of CIA/NSA Special Collection Service (SCS) [[eavesdropping]] sites in 2004]]
[[File:SCSGlobalPresence.png|thumb|Location and status of CIA/NSA Special Collection Service (SCS) eavesdropping sites as of August 13, 2010]]

The '''Special Collection Service''' ('''SCS''') is a highly classified joint U.S. [[Central Intelligence Agency]]–[[National Security Agency]] program charged with inserting eavesdropping equipment in difficult-to-reach places, such as foreign embassies, communications centers, and foreign government installations. Established in the late 1970s and headquartered in [[Beltsville, Maryland]],<ref>{{cite web |title=Eyeballing the CIA/NSA Special Collection Service |publisher=[[Cryptome]] |url=https://cryptome.org/eyeball/scs/scs-eyeball.htm |date=May 13, 2002 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180609112154/http://cryptome.org/eyeball/scs/scs-eyeball.htm |archive-date=June 9, 2018 |quote=Several years ago, according to sources, SCS relocated to a new, 300-acre, three-building complex disguised as a corporate campus and shielded by a dense forest outside Beltsville, Maryland.}}</ref> the SCS has been involved in operations ranging from the [[Cold War]] to hunting [[al-Qaeda]] after the [[September 11 attacks]].

==Mission==
The SCS is a U.S. [[black budget]] program<ref>[http://cdn3.spiegel.de/images/image-561286-galleryV9-snix.jpg Classification Guide 356-01] Accessed October 27, 2013</ref> that has been described as the United States' "''Mission Impossible'' force," responsible for "close surveillance, burglary, wiretapping, breaking and entering."<ref name=lichtblau01>{{cite news |last=Lichtblau |first=Eric |author-link=Eric Lichtblau |title=Spy Suspect May Have Revealed U.S. Bugging; Espionage: Hanssen left signs that he told Russia where top-secret overseas eavesdropping devices are placed, officials say |newspaper=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=February 28, 2001 |page=A1 นิเจ้าบ๊องต๋อยเซมเบ้|url=http://www.latimes.com/news/nation/updates2/lat_spy010228.htm |archive-date=April 17, 2001 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20010417230720/http://www.latimes.com/news/nation/updates2/lat_spy010228.htm}}</ref><ref name=lathem01>{{cite news |last=Lathem |first=Niles |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211112101428/https://nypost.com/2001/03/01/feds-to-offer-fbi-mole-sing-or-die-deal/ |archive-date=November 12, 2021}}</ref><ref name=today01>{{cite episode Hanssen Later This Week |series=Today |series-link=Today (U.S. TV program) |network=[[NBC]] |airdate=February 27, 2001 |url=http://www.globalsecurity.org/org/news/2001/010227-spy.htm}}</ref><ref name=kaihla01>{{cite news |last=Kaihla |first=Paul |title=Weapons of the Secret War |newspaper=[[Business 2.0]] |date=November 2001 |url=http://www.business20.com/articles/mag/print/0,1643,17511,FF.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20031004032408/http://www.business20.com/articles/mag/print/0,1643,17511,FF.html |archive-date=October 4, 2003 |url-status=dead}}</ref> It is headquartered in Beltsville, Maryland, in an obscured building that was at one time labeled simply "CSSG" and is sometimes designated as "F6".<ref name="week">{{cite magazine |url=http://theweek.com/articles/476482/inside-secret-world-americas-eavesdropping-spies |title=Inside the secret world of America's top eavesdropping spies |first=David W. |last=Brown |magazine=[[The Week (magazine)|The Week]] |date=April 12, 2012}}</ref>  Next door is the [[U.S. Department of State]]'s [[Beltsville Information Management Center]], to which the SCS is linked via fiber optic cable. The SCS is jointly staffed by the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and the National Security Agency (NSA).<ref name=kaihla01 /><ref name=fas1>{{cite web |last=Pike |first=John |title=CIA/NSA CSSG Special Collection Service, "Communiciations Support Group," 11600 Springfield Rd, Beltsville, MD |publisher=[[Federation of American Scientists]] |date=April 28, 1996 |url=https://fas.org/irp/facility/cssg.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20010803063040/https://fas.org/irp/facility/cssg.htm |archive-date=August 3, 2001 |url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name=fp12>{{cite magazine |last=Aid |first=Matthew M. |author-link=Matthew Aid |title=The Spies Next Door: The top 10 Beltway intel centers hiding in plain sight |magazine=[[Foreign Policy (magazine)|Foreign Policy]] |date=September 21, 2012 |url=https://foreignpolicy.com/articles/2012/09/21/the_spies_next_door |access-date=July 6, 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-date=February 25, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140225183404/https://foreignpolicy.com/articles/2012/09/21/the_spies_next_door}}</ref> According to intelligence historian [[James Bamford]], "The position of SCS chief alternates between NSA and CIA officials."<ref name=bamford08 /> SCS operatives are based out of U.S. embassies and consulates overseas, and operatives often use [[United States Foreign Service|Foreign Service]] or [[Diplomatic Telecommunications Service]] cover when deployed.<ref name=kaihla01 /><ref name=bamford01>{{cite interview |last=Bamford |first=James |author-link=James Bamford |interviewer=[[Brian Lamb]] |title=Booknotes |publisher=[[C-SPAN]] |date=September 16, 2001 |url=http://www.booknotes.org/Watch/166048-1/James+Bamford.aspx |last=Pike |first=John |title=State Department: Beltsville Communications Annex |date=April 28, 1996 |publisher=[[Federation of American Scientists]] |url=https://fas.org/irp/facility/odell.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20010803054524/https://fas.org/irp/facility/odell.htm |archive-date=August 3, 2001 |url-status=dead}}</ref> Their mission is to intercept sensitive information on espionage, nuclear arms, terrorist networks, drug trafficking and other national-security-related issues.<ref name=lichtblau01 />

The SCS was established to overcome a problem in that the NSA typically intercepts communications "passively" from its various intercept facilities throughout the world, yet the increasing sophistication of foreign communications equipment renders passive interception futile and instead requires direct access to the communications equipment. The CIA, meanwhile, has access to agents specializing in clandestine operations and thus is more able to gain access to foreign communication equipment, yet lacks the NSA's expertise in communications eavesdropping. Hence, the SCS was born, combining the communications intelligence capabilities of the NSA with the covert action capabilities of the CIA in order to facilitate access to sophisticated foreign communications systems.<ref name=lichtblau01 /><ref name=isnard00>{{cite news |last=Isnard |first=Jacques |title=Une alliance secrète entre la NSA et la CIA |date=February 23, 2000 |newspaper=[[Le Monde]] |language=fr |trans-title=A Secret Alliance Between the CIA and the NSA |url=https://www.lemonde.fr/archives/article/2000/02/23/une-alliance-secrete-entre-la-nsa-et-la-cia_3592908_1819218.html |url-access=subscription |url-status=live |archive-date=September 30, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240930163914/https://www.lemonde.fr/archives/article/2000/02/23/une-alliance-secrete-entre-la-nsa-et-la-cia_3592908_1819218.html}}</ref><ref name=bowman02>{{cite news |last=Bowman |first=Tom |author-link=Tom Bowman (journalist) |title=Report faults decisions by intelligence agencies; Management actions in allocating resources are blamed in Sept. 11 |newspaper=[[Baltimore Sun]] |date=July 18, 2002 |page=3A}}</ref>

The SCS employs exotic [[covert listening device]] technologies to bug foreign embassies, communications centers, computer facilities, fiber-optic networks, and government installations.<ref name=lichtblau01 /><ref name=lathem01 /> The U.S. government has never officially acknowledged its existence, and little is known about the technologies and techniques it employs.<ref name=lichtblau01 /> The sole inside account of SCS comes from a [[Canadians|Canadian]], Mike Frost, whose 1994 book ''Spyworld'' revealed that the program was known to insiders at the time as "College Park".<ref name=roslin01>{{cite news |last=Roslin |first=Alex |title=Cyberspies and saboteurs: Hackers on the payroll of U.S. security agencies |newspaper=[[The Gazette (Montreal)|The Gazette]] |location=[[Montreal]] |date=October 6, 2001 |page=A1 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20011216183808/http://www.canada.com/montreal/montrealgazette/story.asp?id=%7B00D3AF24-9BFD-403A-AF2C-A6C9501EEC13%7D |archive-date=December 16, 2001 |url=http://www.canada.com/montreal/montrealgazette/story.asp?id=%7b00D3AF24-9BFD-403A-AF2C-A6C9501EEC13%7d |url-status=dead }}</ref> As of 2008, the SCS is reported to target for recruitment key foreign communications personnel such as database managers, systems administrators, and [[information technology]] specialists.<ref name=bamford08>{{cite book |last=Bamford |first=James |author-link=James Bamford |title=The Shadow Factory: The Ultra-Secret NSA from 9/11 to the Eavesdropping on America |publisher=Knopf Doubleday Publishing Group |year=2008 |isbn=9780385521321 |url-access=registration |url=https://archive.org/details/shadowfactory00bamf }}</ref>

During October 2013, reports by former NSA contractor [[Edward Snowden]] led to the unveiling of the SCS having systematically wiretapped [[Chancellor of Germany]] [[Angela Merkel]]'s private cell phone over a period of over 10 years, which among other activities to wiretap and systematically record large amounts of European and South American leaders' and citizens' communication by the NSA led to a distinct diplomatic backlash at the United States government.<ref>[https://www.spiegel.de/international/germany/cover-story-how-nsa-spied-on-merkel-cell-phone-from-berlin-embassy-a-930205.html "Embassy Espionage: The NSA's Secret Spy Hub in Berlin"] ''Der Spiegel'', 27 October 2013</ref>

==History==

===Background===

The SCS program was established in 1978 during the Cold War between the [[United States]] and the [[Soviet Union]].<ref name="week"/><ref name=lichtblau01 /><ref name=roslin01 />

As [[encryption]] technology increased in sophistication, by the end of the 20th century many coded signals proved unbreakable. Due to this problem, bugging techniques and technologies saw a revival: unable to easily intercept and decrypt foreign communications through passive means, the U.S. government needed to instead intercept the communications at their source, and thus the SCS program was expanded in the 1990s to fulfill this need.<ref name=diamond99>{{cite news |last=Diamond |first=John |title=To Catch a Spy Because the FBI Noted Inept Actions of a Russian Near the State Department, Espionage Was Uncovered |newspaper=[[Chicago Tribune]] |date=December 10, 1999 |pages=1, 1:2}}</ref><ref name=loeb01>{{cite news |last=Loeb |first=Vernon |author-link=Vernon Loeb |title=Test Of Strength; For two years, Air Force general Michael Hayden has waged a secret struggle to overhaul the world's most powerful spy agency. Nothing's riding on his success but the future of America's national security |newspaper=[[Washington Post Magazine]] |date=July 29, 2001 |page=9}}</ref><ref name=finder01>{{cite news |last=Finder |first=Joseph |author-link=Joseph Finder |title=Bugging the World |newspaper=[[New York Times Book Review]] |date=April 29, 2001 |page=9}}</ref>

===Snowden Leak===

According to documents leaked by [[Edward Snowden]], the SCS is part of a larger [[global surveillance]] program known as [[Stateroom (surveillance program)|STATEROOM]].<ref>{{cite news|last=[[Laura Poitras]], Marcel Rosenbach and Holger Stark|title=Codename 'Apalachee': How America Spies on Europe and the UN|url=http://www.spiegel.de/international/world/secret-nsa-documents-show-how-the-us-spies-on-europe-and-the-un-a-918625-2.html|work=[[Der Spiegel]]|date=August 26, 2013 |access-date=December 22, 2013}}</ref>

==Activities==

===Cold War===
SCS operatives reportedly hid eavesdropping devices in [[pigeon]]s perched on the windowsills of the [[Embassy of Russia in Washington, D.C.|Soviet Embassy]] in [[Washington, D.C.]]<ref name=kaihla01 />

===Infiltration===
The SCS program was compromised by infamous [[Federal Bureau of Investigation]] (FBI) mole [[Robert Hanssen]] in the 1990s, which provided [[Moscow]] with sensitive information about highly sophisticated U.S. overseas bugging operations.<ref name=lathem01 /><ref name=masters01>{{cite news |last1=Masters |first1=Brooke A. |last2=Pincus |first2=Walter |author-link2=Walter Pincus |title=Spy-Case Indictment Postponed; Two Sides Cooperating; Suspect Gets Access to Evidence |newspaper=[[Washington Post]] |date=March 2, 2001 |page=A8}}</ref> However, the program was so secret that, after Hanssen's arrest, the FBI would only describe it in general terms, as a "program of enormous value, expense, and importance to the U.S. government".<ref name=lichtblau01 /><ref name=today01 />

===Afghanistan===
In 1999, as the [[Clinton Administration]] sought to kill [[Osama bin Laden]] following the [[1998 U.S. embassy bombings]], SCS operatives covertly entered [[Afghanistan]] to place eavesdropping devices within range of [[al-Qaeda]]'s tactical radios.<ref name=gellman01>{{cite news |last=Gellman |first=Barton |author-link=Barton Gellman |title=Broad Effort Launched After '98 Attacks |newspaper=[[Washington Post]] |date=December 19, 2001 |page=A1}}</ref>

===China===
The SCS was rumored to have been involved in the 2001 operation that planted 27 satellite-controlled bugs in the [[Boeing 767-300ER]] that was to be used as Chinese leader [[Jiang Zemin]]'s official jet. The bugs were discovered, however, before they could be switched on.<ref name=scmp02>{{cite news |title=Air turbulence a test for ties |newspaper=[[South China Morning Post]] |date=January 24, 2002 |page=12}}</ref>

===Iraq War===
Prior to the [[2003 invasion of Iraq|2003 U.S. invasion of Iraq]], SCS was described as the "prime mover" of electronic surveillance in the country.<ref name=vest99>{{cite news |last1=Vest |first1=Jason |last2=Madsen |first2=Wayne |author-link1=Jason Vest |author-link2=Wayne Madsen (journalist) |title=A Most Unusual Collection Agency |newspaper=[[The Village Voice]] |date=March 2, 1999 |url=http://www.villagevoice.com/features/9908/vest_madsen.shtml |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20010815223623/http://www.villagevoice.com/features/9908/vest_madsen.shtml |archive-date=August 15, 2001 |url-status=dead}}</ref> SCS operatives built numerous antennae, spaced throughout the Iraqi countryside, capable of intercepting Iraqi microwave communications. These Iraqi communications would have been otherwise difficult to intercept, because they beamed hilltop to hilltop in a narrow band, with an angle too oblique and thus too dissipated to be intercepted by air or spacecraft.<ref name=gellman99>{{cite news |last=Gellman |first=Barton |author-link=Barton Gellman |title=Barton Gellman: Interview |newspaper=[[Frontline (U.S. TV series)|Frontline]] |publisher=[[PBS]] |date=April 27, 1999 |url=https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/pages/frontline/shows/unscom/interviews/gellman.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121112162116/http://www.pbs.org/wgbh/pages/frontline/shows/unscom/interviews/gellman.html |archive-date=November 12, 2012 |url-status=live}}</ref>

In 1998, the U.S. government recruited an [[Australia]]n operative under SCS and deployed him to Iraq. The operative reported concerns about what was transpiring in Iraq, in that there was "a very high volume of data, and that he was getting no feedback about whether it was good, bad, or useful". He further reported that "this was a massive intelligence collection operation{{snd}} one that was not in accordance with what [[UNSCOM]] was supposed to be doing" at the time.<ref name=vest99 />

After the invasion, SCS operatives were employed in the hunt for [[Saddam Hussein]], planting sophisticated eavesdropping equipment in target areas to intercept communications that were then analyzed by [[voice analysis]] experts.<ref name=mcdougall03>{{cite news |last1=McDougall |first1=Dan |author-link1=Dan McDougall |last2=Ward |first2=Sharon |title=Saddam may have fled as house of cards collapses |newspaper=[[The Scotsman]] |date=April 14, 2003 |page=10}}</ref>

=== Al-Qaeda ===
The SCS was heavily involved in eavesdropping to advance the [[war on terror]], setting up eavesdropping posts around [[Middle East]]ern capitals and figures close to Osama bin Laden's terrorism network.<ref name=kaihla01 /><ref name=bamford07>{{cite book |last=Bamford |first=James |author-link=James Bamford |title=Body of Secrets: Anatomy of the Ultra-Secret National Security Agency |publisher=Random House Digital |year=2007 |isbn=9780307425058 |page=647}}</ref> In 1999, an SCS team monitored al-Qaeda training camps near [[Khost]].<ref name="week"/>

When the United States located [[Osama bin Laden's compound in Abbottabad]], [[Pakistan]], SCS operatives established a base in an apartment that the CIA had rented a mile away from the compound. They focused lasers on the compound windows and, by analyzing the vibrations, were able to count the number of people inside and outside, and also ascertained that there was one person who never ventured outside the compound. Bin Laden was [[Death of Osama bin Laden|killed inside the compound]] during a raid by U.S. special operations forces on May 2, 2011.<ref name=assam11>{{cite news |title=Laden's killing: other side of the story |newspaper=[[Assam Tribune]] |date=June 3, 2011}}</ref><ref name=calvert11>{{cite news |last=Calvert |first=Scott |title=Listening for Bin Laden: the NSA's Intercept of a Phone Call by a Courier May Have Been a Key Piece of Evidence Leading to the Terrorist Leader's Compound |newspaper=[[Baltimore Sun]] |date=May 8, 2011 |page=A1}}</ref>
